subject: arts-crafts
title: Basic Drawing and Color
summary: This chapter introduces students to the basics of drawing and color theory, including primary and secondary colors, drawing simple shapes, nature drawing, and color mixing techniques.

sections.title: Primary and Secondary Colors
sections.content: Colors are an essential part of art and design. The primary colors are red, blue, and yellow, and they cannot be created by mixing other colors. When we mix two primary colors together, we get secondary colors: red and yellow make orange, blue and yellow make green, and red and blue make purple. Understanding the color wheel helps artists choose colors that work well together. In Bangladeshi folk art, bright and vibrant colors are traditionally used to create eye-catching designs.

sections.title: Drawing Basic Shapes
sections.content: Every drawing is built from basic geometric shapes such as circles, squares, triangles, rectangles, and ovals. Learning to draw these shapes accurately is the foundation of all artwork. Students should practice drawing these shapes freehand until they can create them smoothly and confidently. Once basic shapes are mastered, they can be combined to draw more complex objects like houses, trees, animals, and human figures.

sections.title: Nature Drawing
sections.content: Nature drawing involves observing and sketching elements from the natural world such as flowers, leaves, trees, fruits, and animals. Bangladesh has a rich variety of natural subjects for drawing, including the shapla (water lily), mango leaves, paddy fields, and various birds. When drawing from nature, students should first observe the object carefully, note its shape and proportions, then sketch the basic outline before adding details. Nature drawing develops observation skills and an appreciation for the beauty of the environment.

sections.title: Color Mixing
sections.content: Color mixing is the technique of combining different colors to create new shades and tones. By adding white to a color, we create a lighter shade called a tint, and by adding black, we create a darker shade called a shade. Mixing complementary colors (colors opposite each other on the color wheel) produces neutral browns and grays. Watercolor and poster paint are common mediums for practicing color mixing in Bangladeshi schools. Experimenting with color mixing helps students understand how colors behave and how to achieve the exact shade they need.
